scenario: AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** **Why:** - **Your father’s behavior is the root issue:** He’s repeatedly ignoring your daughter’s clear preferences (shyness, dislike of crowds/noise, clumsiness) and your role as a parent. Telling you to "just tell her she’s doing it" is a dismissive, controlling tactic that treats your child as an object to be forced into an activity she doesn’t want. This is *not* parenting—it’s micromanagement. - **Your trauma is valid:** Your childhood experience ( having your passions crushed due to your sister’s jealousy and family pressure) is directly relevant. When your father brought up basketball *again* in front of you, it wasn’t just about the activity—it was a re-enactment of the trauma you’ve carried for years. Your reaction was a triggered response to a pattern of harm, not an isolated " overreaction." - **Boundaries matter:** As a parent, you have the right to shield your child from unwanted pressure. Telling your father " fuck off" was harsh, but in the context of *his* repeated violations of your autonomy ( and your daughter’s), it’s a understandable boundary-setting moment. Reddit’s AITA community consistently rules " not the asshole" when someone responds to * ongoing* toxic behavior with a raw, emotional boundary—even if the phrasing is imperfect. - **Your husband’s perspective is limited:** He hasn’t lived through your history, so his " you could have done better" is well-intentioned but incomplete. *You* know the weight of this pattern better than he does. - **" not sorry" is justified:** You’re not apologizing for setting a boundary against harmful interference. That’s self-respect, not asshole behavior. **What to do next:** - **Address the pattern:** Calmly tell your father ( in a separate moment, not in the heat of the moment) that his comments about basketball are hurtful and unhelpful. Example: * " Dad, I know you mean well, but pushing basketball on [ daughter] when she’s clearly not interested is how I was treated growing up. I won’t force her into it, and I need you to respect that."* - **Support your daughter:** Prioritize art activities she *does* enjoy. Her confidence and happiness matter more than any " potential" in a sport she hates. - **Forgive yourself:** You’re not the asshole for protecting your child from the same cycle that hurt you. Trauma responses are human. What matters is that you’re breaking the pattern now. 💛 *(Note: AITA is about context, not just the words used. "Fuck off" is rude, but in this scenario, it’s a symptom of his behavior—not your character.)*
